cards.front: Recall a key point about Recruitment and Selection
cards.back: Internal recruitment fills vacancies from within the business (promotion, transfer): quicker, cheaper, motivating for staff, but limits the talent pool and may cause resentment if not transparent.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Recruitment and Selection
cards.back: External recruitment brings in new people from outside: wider talent pool, fresh ideas, but more expensive and time-consuming (advertising, interviewing) and may demotivate existing staff who wanted the role.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Recruitment and Selection
cards.back: A job description lists the duties and responsibilities of the role; a person specification lists the skills, qualifications, and experience required. Both are essential for fair, effective recruitment.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Recruitment and Selection
cards.back: Selection methods: interviews (most common but subjective), application forms/CVs (screening), assessment centres (observe candidates in tasks), aptitude tests (measure specific skills), and references (verify candidate claims).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Recruitment and Selection
cards.back: The recruitment process: identify vacancy → write job description and person specification → advertise → shortlist → interview/assess → appoint → induct. Each stage has legal requirements (equality, non-discrimination).

cards.front: What should you know about business exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating recruitment methods, use the CQR framework: Cost (how much does the process cost?), Quality (does it find the best candidate?), Risk (what if the wrong person is hired?). A bad recruitment decision costs far more than a thorough recruitment process.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: External recruitment is always better because it brings in fresh ideas. Correct: External recruitment can bring fresh ideas but also carries risks: the candidate may not fit the culture, takes longer to become productive (learning curve), may leave quickly if the reality doesn't match the interview, and demotivates existing staff who expected promotion.
